summary_grc: οἱ χοροὶ ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ ἀγωνίζονται· ὁ ἄρχων τῷ χορηγῷ τὸν τρίποδα δίδωσιν, ὁ δὲ χορηγὸς αὐτὸν τῷ θεῷ τίθησιν.
summary_en: The second day: the dithyramb contest of the tribes, the choregos who pays for it, and the bronze tripod that is the prize. Who gives and puts what where: δίδωμι, τίθημι (and ἵημι), the three uses of αὐτός, and adjectives like ταχύς.

grammar.md:
**-μι verbs: δίδωμι and τίθημι.** Most verbs you know end in -ω. A small, very common group ends in **-μι** and puts the endings straight onto the stem, without a linking vowel. You have met ἵσταμαι and δύναμαι; now the two most useful active ones: **δίδωμι** 'give' and **τίθημι** 'put, place'. Both double their first consonant in the present (δι-δω-, τι-θη-), and both have a **long** vowel in the singular and a **short** one in the plural.

| | δίδωμι *give* | τίθημι *put* |
|---|---|---|
| I | δίδω**μι** | τίθη**μι** |
| you | δίδω**ς** | τίθη**ς** |
| he, she | δίδω**σι(ν)** | τίθη**σι(ν)** |
| we | δίδο**μεν** | τίθε**μεν** |
| you (pl.) | δίδο**τε** | τίθε**τε** |
| they | διδό**ασι(ν)** | τιθέ**ασι(ν)** |
| imperfect | ἐδίδουν, ἐδίδους, ἐδίδου … ἐδίδοσαν | ἐτίθην, ἐτίθεις, ἐτίθει … ἐτίθεσαν |
| infinitive | διδόναι | τιθέναι |
| participle | διδούς, διδοῦσα, διδόν | τιθείς, τιθεῖσα, τιθέν |
| imperative | δίδου, δίδοτε | τίθει, τίθετε |

The **future** is regular: δώσω, θήσω. The **aorist** has -κα in the singular and the short stem in the plural: **ἔδωκα**, ἔδωκας, **ἔδωκε(ν)**, ἔδομεν, ἔδοτε, ἔδοσαν; ἔθηκα, ἔθηκας, ἔθηκε(ν), ἔθεμεν, ἔθετε, ἔθεσαν. Outside the indicative the aorist is short and very common: infinitive **δοῦναι**, θεῖναι; participle **δούς**, θείς; imperative **δός!** 'give!', **θές!** 'put!'. **ἵημι** 'send, let go, throw' goes like τίθημι: ἵησι(ν), ἱᾶσι(ν); aorist ἧκα. Compounds keep the pattern: **προστίθημι** 'add', ἀνατίθημι 'dedicate'.

**αὐτός: three uses, one word.**

| use | position | example |
|---|---|---|
| *him, her, it, them* | alone, not first in its clause | τὸ πρόσωπον **αὐτοῦ** 'his face' |
| *-self* (intensive) | with a noun or pronoun, outside the article | **αὐτὸς** τὸ ἀργύριον δίδωσιν 'he gives the money himself'; ὁ θεὸς **αὐτός** |
| *the same* | after the article | ἐν **τῷ αὐτῷ** χορῷ 'in the same chorus' |

**Adjectives like ταχύς.** ταχύς 'quick' has a third-declension masculine and neuter in -υς/-υ (stem ταχε-) and a first-declension feminine in -εῖα:

| | m | f | n |
|---|---|---|---|
| nom. | ταχ**ύς** | ταχ**εῖα** | ταχ**ύ** |
| gen. | ταχ**έος** | ταχ**είας** | ταχ**έος** |
| dat. | ταχ**εῖ** | ταχ**είᾳ** | ταχ**εῖ** |
| acc. | ταχ**ύν** | ταχ**εῖαν** | ταχ**ύ** |
| nom. pl. | ταχ**εῖς** | ταχ**εῖαι** | ταχ**έα** |

Its comparison is irregular: **θάττων** 'quicker', **τάχιστος** 'quickest'. Others like it: βραδύς 'slow', βαρύς 'heavy', ἡδύς 'sweet', εὐθύς 'straight'.

**ἕτερος, ἀμφότεροι, ἅπας.** ἕτερος is 'the other (of two)', or 'another': δός μοι καὶ **ἑτέραν**. ἀμφότεροι 'both' stands in predicate position: **ἀμφότεροι** οἱ χοροί. ἅπας, ἅπασα, ἅπαν is a stronger πᾶς: **ἅπαντες** 'all together, every one of them'.

culture.title: Choruses, choregoi and the tripod
culture.md: The second great event of the City Dionysia was the contest of **dithyrambs**, songs for Dionysus sung and danced in a circle round the aulos player. Each of the ten tribes of Kleisthenes entered a chorus of fifty men and one of fifty boys, so a thousand citizens sang in a single day. Nobody was paid to perform, but somebody had to pay for the training, the costumes and the aulos player: this was the **choregia** (χορηγία), one of the *liturgies* the city laid on its richest men instead of a regular tax. A choregos for a boys' dithyramb might spend 1,500 drachmas or more, and ambitious men spent lavishly, because a victory brought public honour and votes in the Assembly. The choregos of the winning chorus received a **bronze tripod** and dedicated it to Dionysus, usually on a monument in the street that ran round the east side of the Acropolis to the theatre, known simply as the Tripods (οἱ Τρίποδες); an inscription recorded the tribe, the choregos, the aulos player and the poet. Victory was decided by ten judges, one from each tribe, whose names had been drawn by lot; each wrote his order of merit on a tablet, the tablets went into an urn, and the archon drew out only five of them, so that neither bribery nor favour could be sure of the result. Dropping sweets and dried figs to the audience, as Theophilos does here, was a trick Aristophanes mocks in his comedies.
